title: The greatest gift
hookLine: above all, the gift of the Name

cards: On some strings of prayer beads, one bead is different from the rest: bigger, or set apart, or with a tassel. You start from it and finish at it, and your fingers know when they've reached it without looking.
The Ardas's list of gifts works the same way. Sikhi, kes, rahit, bibek, visaah, bharosaa: six gifts, each one precious.
Then one more, marked out from all the others with a single phrase, so that no one could mistake which one matters most.

teach.h: DAANAAN SIR DAAN: THE CROWN OF GIFTS.
teach.b: After the six gifts, the Ardas says: daanaan sir daan, naam daan. The gift at the head of all gifts: the gift of the Name. Sir is the head, the top, the crown: the gift that crowns the others.
Naam, the Name, has come up many times on this path. It isn't only a word for God.
It's God's presence, known and remembered, filling a life. Why is it above discipline, discernment, trust and faith?

teach.h: THE SOURCE OF THE OTHER SIX.
teach.b: Because, Sikhs would say, it's the source of them. Think back to chit, two days ago: may Waheguru come to mind, and by that, every joy.

And Guru Tegh Bahadur's last salok: I have held the Name in my heart; nothing equals it. The Ardas says the same thing a third way. Of everything that can be given, it names this one to ask for and want most.
The word daan has a second edge, too.

teach.h: RECEIVED AS A GIFT, SHOWN IN GIVING.
teach.b: Here it means a gift received.
But Gurbani also groups three words, naam, daan, ishnaan: the Name, giving, and cleansing. There, daan means giving to others. So the Name is a gift you receive, and a life of giving is how it shows.
Some Sikhs also speak of the amrit ceremony as receiving naam daan, the gift of the Name, from the Panj Pyare. In a ceremony or in the quiet of a morning, the Ardas asks for it as a gift.
In this teaching, nobody earns the Name. They ask for it, and they receive it.

how: At the end of the Ardas's list of gifts, Sikhs ask for daanaan sir daan naam daan, the gift of the Name above all gifts; some also speak of receiving naam at the amrit ceremony.

o: the gift of the Name, the crown of gifts
the naming ceremony for a newborn baby
a donation of money given in God's name

games.q: the greatest gift — tap the pairs.
p: the gift at the head of gifts

s: the Ardas ranks the gift of the Name above the other gifts
daanaan sir daan: the gift that crowns them all.
in Sikh teaching, the Name is earned by effort
in the Ardas it's asked for and received as a gift.
daan can mean both a gift received and giving to others
in naam, daan, ishnaan it means giving.

games.q: you can ask for only one gift today: discipline, discernment, trust, or the Name. which does the Ardas put first?
o: discipline, because it keeps the others.
the Name, because the others come from it.
games.why: daanaan sir daan naam daan: the Name is the head of all gifts, and Sikhs say it's the source of the rest.

practice: Picture a string of beads in your hand, and let your fingers find the one that's different. If you pray, ask simply for naam daan, the gift of the Name, then say Waheguru slowly, letting it fill the time.
If you don't, ask what you'd put at the head of your own list, the one gift above the others, and sit with it.

wordCard.voice: Naam daan. Daanaan sir daan: the gift at the head of all gifts, the gift of the Name.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: naam daan, the gift of the Name, called the gift at the head of all gifts.

carryVoice: Your line: the name above all. One bead, set apart from all the rest. See you tomorrow.
